label: Some Closedness Criteria
notes: Open by naming the section as a qualification toolkit. Convexity itself survives many algebraic operations, but closedness asks whether limiting boundary points survive the same operation. The lecture will keep returning to one diagnostic question: can a convergent image be produced by source points escaping to infinity?

label: Why Closedness Can Fail
notes: Contrast relative interiors with closures before stating any test. Relative interiors behave almost functorially under linear maps, while closure has only a one-sided inclusion. That gap is not technical bookkeeping; it is the place where missing endpoints, nonattained infima, and lower semi-continuity failures appear.

label: Projection Warning
notes: Use the hyperbolic epigraph as the basic warning. The set is closed because no finite point sits over u equals zero, but the projection records only positive u values. The sequence u equals one over n approaches the missing endpoint while the forgotten coordinate goes to infinity.

label: Relative Interior Qualification
notes: This is the first positive qualification. A shared relative-interior point lets closure be tested by radial limits from a genuine interior anchor. For function sums and suprema, the anchor prevents the operation from being supported only at incompatible boundary pieces.

label: Recession Cone Test
notes: State the root test in operational language. A linear image loses closedness when a recession direction is invisible to the map and is not reversible lineality. If every killed recession direction is reversible, or if the kernel meets the recession cone only at zero, the image cannot hide escape to infinity.

label: Sum Closedness
notes: Explain the sum rule by reducing it to the root test. Put the product set in the source and use the addition map. A null direction for the addition map is precisely a cancellation among recession directions, so closedness is protected when cancellations are only lineality.

label: Linear Image Closedness
notes: Turn the theorem into a checklist an analyst can use. First close the source if needed, then inspect recession directions, then intersect them with the kernel of the map. The quotient by lineality is the reason reversible directions are harmless while one-way directions create missing limits.

label: Cone Criteria
notes: Cones make the recession bookkeeping visible because the set already equals its own recession model. The section uses this to close sums of cones, to describe the closure of a generated cone, and to show why bounded generators away from the origin are a safe special case.

label: Epigraph Perspective
notes: Move from sets to functions by looking at epigraphs. The infimal image Ah is closed when the epigraph image is closed and has no downward vertical recession. That same condition gives attainment, because each vertical fiber over y then meets the epigraph in a closed lower half-line.

label: Counterexample Lab
notes: Invite students to modify the bad example rather than just memorize it. Bounding the forgotten coordinate, removing the vertical recession direction, or projecting along a different map repairs the pathology. Leaving the upward null recession direction in place keeps the missing endpoint.

label: Certificate Graph
notes: Use the graph to organize the section. Theorem 9.1 is the source certificate; the sum and cone statements are direct set consequences; the epigraph image theorem powers lower semi-continuity and existence; the relative-interior branch supplies closure formulas when functions are not already closed.

label: Numerical Closure Probe
notes: Show how little numerical evidence is needed to reveal the phenomenon. The sequence of feasible points has projections tending to zero, but no sampled or exact point realizes zero. The JSON check is not a proof of the theorem; it is a compact audit trail for the core invariant.

label: Rule Ledger
notes: Read the ledger as a decision table for future proofs. Each row says which operation is being used, what hidden escape direction must be excluded, and what conclusion becomes available. The recurring pattern is to replace vague compactness hopes with a precise recession or relative-interior qualification.

label: Recap
notes: Close by asking students to diagnose closedness before assuming it. For a new image, sum, epigraph projection, cone, or hull, identify the operation, test recession directions killed by the operation, check for a relative-interior anchor when functions are involved, and then state the closedness conclusion.
